input.rationale: The install-snapshot rewind question is the only open lead, and its discriminator needs the real replication path rather than more reading. The probe drives three isolation/compaction/reconnect rounds, watches every node's applied index and snapshot index every 2ms, and emits the operands (prior and new applied index, snapshot index, log store last index) for the recovered node and for nodes that never show the install signature, so the controller's execution can decide between a rewinding install and monotone applied state.

limitations: Source-only so far, plus one native local run of the probe (not retained evidence) in which the recovered node reached the install signature (snapshot index 257 above log store last index 197 over 1234 poll ticks) while no node showed an applied-index decrease.
The probe can only refute the concern for the scenarios it drives; it cannot prove unreachability across configurations where the leader's latest snapshot index is below a follower's applied index.
No defect is claimed while the question is open.
resume_conditions: Resume when the controller has executed the requested probe (assurance_install_rewind.go) so the rewind question is judged from retained observations.
Resume earlier if source shows a receiver-side index check or a maintained invariant that the log always covers (lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied], which would refute the concern without execution.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with SnapshotInterval=30ms, SnapshotThreshold=10 and TrailingLogs=5, running three rounds of: 25 warm commands, isolate one follower, 60 further commands by the remaining quorum, reconnect, then 1.2s of polling every 2ms that records each node's applied index, snapshot index and log store last index.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) with the settings above performs real bootstrap, replication, snapshotting and compaction through the in-memory transport.

Isolating one follower leaves the leader with a quorum, so commits continue and the leader's log compacts past that follower's next index, making the follower recover through the real InstallSnapshot handler on reconnect.
Polling every 2ms is dense enough to observe an applied-index decrease if one occurs, because an install sets lastApplied directly from the request.

The install signature (snapshot index above the log store last index) identifies a node that has been through InstallSnapshot or is in the post-install state; nodes without it are the steadier comparison within the same execution.
excluded: Configurations where the leader's latest snapshot index is below a follower's applied index, which the probe does not deliberately construct.
Monotonic log store implementations, which take the removeOldLogs branch.
Client-visible consequences of a hypothetical rewind and any performance measurement.

experiment.prefix: The harness builds everything with captured test facilities and real producers: MakeCluster(3, conf) with SnapshotInterval=30ms, SnapshotThreshold=10, TrailingLogs=5 bootstraps the cluster and Elects a leader; each round applies 25 commands through leader.Apply, chooses the lexicographically first follower, records its applied index, snapshot index and log store last index, cuts it off with c.Disconnect, commits 60 further commands through the remaining quorum, reconnects with c.FullyConnect, and then polls all three nodes every 2ms for 1.2s. During polling the harness tracks each node's maximum applied index, any applied-index decrease with the snapshot index and log store last index at that moment, the number of snapshot-index changes, and how many poll ticks showed the snapshot index above the log store last index (the install signature). probe_start and one round_start per round record the scenario operands; per node the harness emits recovered_node_probe_end when the install signature was seen and steady_node_probe_end otherwise, carrying max_applied_seen, applied_at_end, observed_applied_decrease, decrease_count, the prior and new applied index and the snapshot/log index at the decrease, snapshot_index_changes, install_signature_ticks and the end state. No storage is pre-filled and no production code is modified.
experiment.requirement: No InstallSnapshot delivered in this scenario moves a receiver's applied index backwards: a request whose snapshot index is below the receiver's applied state would show up as an applied-index decrease with the snapshot index below the previously observed applied index, and the receiver's applied index must stay monotone across the isolation, compaction and recovery rounds.
experiment.responsibility: Receiver-side admission and applied-state bookkeeping of InstallSnapshot (lastApplied set from the request, snapshot index, log store range) observed through the values the node reports while the leader drives real installs.

comparisons.description: Recovered node: having been through the install path during the rounds, its applied index never moved backwards, so no delivered snapshot was older than its applied state in this execution.

Same-execution comparison: nodes that never showed the install signature kept applied state monotone as well, so a decrease would have to be attributed to the install path rather than to polling or snapshotting in general.

investigations.question: In the captured snapshot, is a leadership-transfer order (TimeoutNow) bound at the receiver to the current leader's authority, or can a delivered order that carries no term and whose claimed sender is not the current leader (and not a configuration member) drive a stable follower out of Follower and depose the serving leader?
investigations.hypothesis: Raft.timeoutNow is the only RPC handler that changes authority without consulting any term: it does setLeader("",""), setState(Candidate) and candidateFromLeadershipTransfer.Store(true) and responds, ignoring RPCHeader.ID/Addr and the configuration. TimeoutNowRequest embeds only RPCHeader, so no term/freshness value exists to check, while the producer only sends it after it has caught the target up (nextIndex beyond the leader's last index) - a precondition the receiver cannot verify. The Candidate run skips pre-vote (raft.go:294-298) and voters skip the known-leader rejection for LeadershipTransfer candidates (raft.go:1645-1656), so the order withdraws both disruption guards at once.
investigations.discriminator: In one fault-free, normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with a stable leader at a known term, deliver a single TimeoutNow to a follower using a transport RPC header whose ID is not a configuration member (and which necessarily carries no term), then observe the target's state/term and the previous leader's state/term for a bounded interval. Control: the same non-member sender with a RequestVoteRequest that does carry a term, but an older one, must leave the target unchanged. If the TimeoutNow leaves the target in Follower at the same term and the leader in place, the hypothesis is refuted; if the target leaves Follower at a higher term while the leader steps down, the receiver-side authority gap is observed.
limitations: The witness is one execution of one fault-free in-process cluster; it establishes the receiver-side transition, not how long clients stayed without a leader afterwards.

Safety was not violated in this execution and is not claimed to be: term/vote rules still select the leader. The defect is the acceptance of a leadership-transfer order that is bound neither to the sender's identity/term nor to its configuration membership.

Because the order carries no term, a replayed or delayed order from a legitimate former leader is indistinguishable from the witness message at the receiver; the witness does not separate those two producers.

investigations.question: Can a server in the captured snapshot hold a configurations.latest (and hence GetConfiguration) that is older than its own committed log, and how is that state produced?
investigations.hypothesis: Re-scoped after reading the FSM apply path: configuration entries never reach FSM.Apply (fsm.go:105-118), so the captured helper's FSM comparison cannot show that a peer holds a configuration entry. The remaining question is whether the >5s 'peer mismatch' seen locally in TestRaft_ProtocolVersion_Upgrade_2_3 came from a peer not having appended the configuration entry within the EnsureSamePeers window (replication lag), or from a server whose configurations.latest/atomic latestConfiguration was reset behind an entry it already holds.
investigations.discriminator: Replay the captured upgrade scenario with per-node instrumentation that records, each 100ms, whether the configuration entry is present in each log store, each node's latestIndex/latestConfiguration, and the leader's per-peer replication nextIndex/lastContact. Lag shows as the entry absent from that peer's log store (with the leader committing via another peer); an internal reset shows as the entry present while latestIndex/latestConfiguration stay below it. A decisive witness needs the entry present and latest still behind after the leader's replication has advanced past it.
limitations: No execution receipt exists for this question; the negative replay result was local exploration on a scratch copy of the captured package, not the controller's fixed-input execution.
The captured failure (peer mismatch after a full 5s EnsureSamePeers window, testing.go:733-752) is a real local observation, but its cause is not established.
resume_conditions: Resume when a harness can emit both per-node log-store contents and configuration state during a run that reproduces the >5s mismatch, or when a concrete producer of a missed configuration append is identified in source.
A reproduction must also record the leader's replication nextIndex/lastContact for the lagging peer, since the earlier local reproduction converged within 250ms and could not separate lag from reset.

gaps.question: Under instrumented replay of the captured upgrade scenario, does any node hold configurations.latest/latestIndex below its own appended configuration entry index for longer than the 5s EnsureSamePeers window, and if so which source path (appendEntries rollback, duplicate-skip in appendEntries, snapshot install, or restart replay) produced it?

history.question: Can a server in the captured snapshot hold a configurations.latest (and hence GetConfiguration) that is older than its own committed log, and how is that state produced?
history.hypothesis: GetConfiguration returns the atomically published latest configuration (api.go:897-903), a value written only by setLatestConfiguration. In the captured package's own TestRaft_ProtocolVersion_Upgrade_2_3, an old follower was observed reporting the 2-server bootstrap configuration for at least the full 5s EnsureSamePeers window while the newly added server reported the 3-server configuration, i.e. the membership read diverged from the replicated configuration entry. A candidate production path is the rollback in appendEntries (raft.go:1526-1532, setLatestConfiguration(committed, committedIndex)) combined with the duplicate-skip loop that never re-runs processConfigurationLogEntry for an entry already present.

limitations: Local exploration only: the captured TestRaft_ProtocolVersion_Upgrade_2_3 failed with 'peer mismatch' in 2 of 3 isolated local runs, but two instrumented re-implementations of the same scenario converged within 250ms on every run, so the mechanism is unresolved rather than established. No knowledge entry is claimed here.
The frozen evidence for any claim must come from the controller's own execution of a fixed harness, which has not been requested for this question.

investigations.question: Does nextConfiguration's AddNonvoter branch silently keep an existing voter's vote (or drop an address update), contradicting the documented contract for AddNonvoter and DemoteVoter, in a way that could let a membership change fail to remove voting authority?
investigations.hypothesis: The branch is asymmetric with AddVoter: when the target server currently has Suffrage != Nonvoter (a voter or staging server) it writes only the address and keeps the existing suffrage, whereas AddVoter replaces the entry when the server is not already a voter. Read alone this looks like a membership change that cannot take authority away.
investigations.discriminator: Compare the branch against the documented contract for AddNonvoter and DemoteVoter and against the captured table expectations for each initial suffrage. A defect requires either a documented promise that AddNonvoter demotes, or a captured expectation showing Voter/Staging becoming Nonvoter; if the documentation assigns demotion to DemoteVoter and the expectations keep Voter/Staging unchanged, the asymmetry is intended behaviour and no authority-loss claim is supported.
limitations: Source-only answer: no execution was requested, so this settles the contract question rather than any live membership-change behaviour.
The captured table expectations cannot distinguish 'address rewritten with the same value' from 'address untouched', so the exact address-update effect on an existing voter was not exercised.

investigations.question: After a configuration entry is committed, can the FSM thread's own applied index lag behind the committed configuration index in a way that makes a snapshot claim an index/configuration combination the FSM does not represent, or that silently mislabels snapshot metadata?
investigations.hypothesis: The FSM thread tracks the index it has accounted for locally and advances it only for entries that actually reach it; configuration entries are dropped before dispatch in protocol <= 2 and, when they do arrive without a ConfigurationStore, return early without advancing the index. That lag is then contained by takeSnapshot, which refuses to snapshot when the FSM index is below the committed configuration index instead of labelling a snapshot with a configuration the FSM never reached.
investigations.discriminator: Trace which log types survive prepareLog into the FSM batch, whether the apply handler advances its local index for each of them, and what takeSnapshot does with the FSM-reported index versus the committed configuration index read afterwards. A defect would require either an entry type that reaches the FSM but silently skips the index bookkeeping without a stated reason, or a snapshot that is created with a configuration index beyond the FSM index.
limitations: Source-only: no execution was requested, so this is a reading of the routing, index and guard code rather than an observed snapshot sequence.
The behaviour is described for the single-apply path; the batching path tracks the last entry in the batch instead (fsm.go:145-171) and was not differentially exercised.

investigations.question: Can shouldSnapshot's unsigned delta between the log store's last index and the last snapshot index underflow, so that the automatic snapshot condition is permanently true on a node whose log store sits below its snapshot index, and what does such a node then do every SnapshotInterval?
investigations.hypothesis: shouldSnapshot computes delta := lastIdx - lastSnap with unsigned integers and no ordering check, where lastIdx is the log store's LastIndex and lastSnap is the snapshot index kept separately. A node that recovered through InstallSnapshot sets its last snapshot index to the snapshot's index, while its log store may keep a lower index: installSnapshot compacts with min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailingLogs), so a node whose log store is below the snapshot index keeps that lower index, and the node's snapshot-aware log index (getLastIndex = max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex)) does not feed shouldSnapshot. If a run reaches that state, delta underflows and the node takes a fresh full-state snapshot every SnapshotInterval until its log store grows past the snapshot index.
investigations.discriminator: Build a cluster whose leader has compacted most of its log, let a fresh or lagging follower recover by InstallSnapshot, and then record, per SnapshotInterval: the follower's log store FirstIndex/LastIndex, its last snapshot index, whether shouldSnapshot returned true, whether takeSnapshot created a new snapshot at the same index and whether a repeat install happened. A confirmed defect needs the log store index below the snapshot index together with repeated snapshot creation on an otherwise idle node; if the log store index is always at or above the snapshot index after install, or if some other producer raises it, the hypothesis is refuted.
limitations: The witness is one bounded window (900ms, SnapshotInterval 40ms, 22 samples) on one recovered node in one cluster; it establishes the condition and the repeated snapshot creation, not production SnapshotInterval cost or how long the condition persists in a busy cluster.

The observation is bounded to the automatic snapshot path on a node isolated from its leader during the window; the receipt does not separate snapshot creations caused by a further InstallSnapshot because isolation excludes that source by construction.

The control comparison in the retained receipt is structurally uncorrelated (both nodes shared one end-event name), so the control is supported by the operands recorded in the same receipt and by the requested successor rather than by a holds outcome.
No safety or availability failure is claimed; the effect is repeated snapshot work, and snapshot retention still bounds how many snapshot objects are kept.

investigations.question: When leadership is lost while a VerifyLeader request is outstanding, can the resulting future be completed twice or left permanently unanswered, given that replication goroutines still hold it and notify it onto the shared verify channel after the leader loop has already responded to the pending set?
investigations.hypothesis: A pending verify future lives in two owners at once: the leader loop's notify set (responded with ErrLeadershipLost by the step-down cleanup) and each replication goroutine's notify map (a separate map, cleared by notifyAll at the end of an RPC). A goroutine that notifies after the cleanup therefore pushes the same future back onto the shared verifyCh, where the follower or candidate loop will respond to it a second time.
investigations.discriminator: Trace who may call respond on a verifyFuture and with what synchronisation, and what happens to a future that a replication goroutine re-notifies after the step-down cleanup: a defect requires two concurrent responders (a data race on the responded flag or a double send on the error channel) or a future that is never completed. If respond is reachable only from the main goroutine holding the run loop, and the second arrival is answered under the same stateless reject rule, the sequence is ordered and idempotent, and the apparent double completion is refuted.
limitations: Source-only: no execution and no race-detector run was requested, so this explains the ownership and ordering rather than observing a concurrent step-down.
The analysis covers verifyFuture completion paths in the captured revision; it says nothing about other future types or about respond callers added later.
The timing window in which a replication goroutine notifies after the cleanup was reasoned from the code, not measured.

investigations.question: Can an InstallSnapshot whose term is current but whose snapshot index is older than the receiving node's applied state rewind that node's applied state, and is the rewind always covered by re-application from the surviving log so that no acknowledged applied entry is lost?
investigations.hypothesis: installSnapshot performs no comparison between the request's LastLogIndex and the receiving node's own lastApplied, last snapshot index or log store range: it rejects only an older term, restores the FSM from the requested snapshot, sets lastApplied and the last snapshot index to the request's values (a decrease when the request is older by index), replaces both configurations from the request, and then compacts or removes old logs according to that index. Recovering from such a rewind therefore depends on processLogs replaying entries from lastApplied+1 out of the surviving log; if the node's log no longer covers (request index, previously applied index] - for example because it had already compacted past the older snapshot index - those already-applied entries cannot be re-applied and the rewound state persists.
investigations.discriminator: Two-sided. Sender side: determine whether a leader can be induced to send a snapshot whose index is below the follower's applied index, given that a snapshot is only opened when the leader cannot produce entries from its nextIndex (below its compacted first index) and that nextIndex only moves on follower responses. Receiver side: instrument a node whose log store first index is above the index of a delivered snapshot and record lastApplied, the FSM-visible applied index and the log first index immediately before and after the install, then whether a later commit advance re-applies the gap. A defect needs a delivered request with snapshot index below the receiver's applied index together with a log that does not cover the gap, so that the applied index is not re-reached; if every delivered request has an index at or above the receiver's applied index, or the surviving log always covers the gap, the concern is refuted.
limitations: Source-only: the handler's lack of an index check is established, but whether a rewinding request is reachable was not established; the send-side argument sketched in the discriminator is a lead, not a proof.

The earlier observation that a node's reported last log index is max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex) and that a follower's applied index never exceeds that reported index narrows the trigger but does not by itself order the leader's snapshot index against the follower's applied index.
No claim is made that this is reachable or that it is a defect; a state regression would also have to survive the log-replay path before it could be called one.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster; one control RPC (stale-term RequestVote from a non-member claimed sender) followed by one TimeoutNow from the same claimed sender to a follower, with bounded observation of target and leader state/term.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) performs real bootstrap: initial configuration entry, leader election and log replication through the in-memory transport.
Both RPCs are delivered over the in-memory transport with no packet loss, reordering or delay, so any observed transition is caused by the delivered request itself.
The sender identity in the RPC header ('ghost-not-in-config') is deliberately not a configuration member; the probe does not rely on the sender being reachable or registered.
The cluster is healthy before the probe: a leader is serving at a known term, which the harness records as steady_state.
excluded: Network-transport authentication, TLS and peer-identity properties outside the Raft layer.
State-machine safety (log matching, single vote per term) and any claim that the newly elected leader violates it.
Behaviour after the observation interval, further elections, and client-visible unavailability.

parameters.control_request_term: target term at steady state minus 1

basis.prefix: The harness builds the prefix itself with the captured test facilities: MakeCluster(3, t, nil) bootstraps a three-voter configuration through the in-memory transport, waits for a stable leader (c.Leader()), and records the leader id/address/term and the chosen follower's state/term as CA_EVENT steady_state. It then selects the follower's transport peer as sender and emits CA_EVENT control_stale_request_vote after delivering a RequestVoteRequest with Term = targetTerm-1 and RPCHeader.ID = 'ghost-not-in-config'. Only then does it deliver the single TimeoutNowRequest with the same RPC header (no term field exists) and emit CA_EVENT after_timeout_now after a bounded 2s observation of the target and the previous leader. No state is injected and no storage is pre-filled.
basis.requirement: A delivered leadership-transfer order is processed as authority to depose the known leader even though the message carries no term and its claimed sender is not the serving leader or a configuration member; the receiver performs no term, identity or membership check before clearing the leader and starting an election.
basis.responsibility: Receiver-side admission of a leadership-transfer order in Raft.timeoutNow, and the two guards that the order disables: the candidate pre-vote gate and the known-leader vote rejection.

comparisons.description: Control: a request that carries a stale term from the same non-member claimed sender is refused and leaves the target in Follower at its original term.
Probe: the delivered order moves the follower out of Follower and raises its term, although the order carries no term and its claimed sender is not the leader or a member.
Probe consequence: the previously serving leader is no longer Leader and reports a higher term within the bounded observation interval.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with a small SnapshotInterval/SnapshotThreshold/TrailingLogs: warm traffic, isolation of one follower, further traffic so the leader compacts, reconnection so the follower recovers by InstallSnapshot, then a bounded idle window on the recovered node (isolated again so no further InstallSnapshot can occur) with the leader observed over the same window as control.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) with SnapshotInterval=40ms, SnapshotThreshold=20, TrailingLogs=5 performs real bootstrap, replication, snapshots and log compaction through the in-memory transport.

Disconnecting only the chosen follower leaves the leader with a quorum (itself plus the other follower), so the cluster keeps committing and the leader's log compacts past the isolated follower's next index.
The isolated follower does not raise its term while isolated because pre-vote is active by default, so reconnecting lets the leader complete the recovery without a spurious election.
Isolating the recovered node again before the window removes the leader as a source of further snapshots, so any new snapshot in that node's store must be produced by its own snapshot goroutine.
Both observed nodes run the same configuration; the leader is idle in the window except for heartbeats.
excluded: Safety claims: no state-machine divergence, lost entry or double application is asserted.
Cost measurement: bytes written, disk wear and FSM Snapshot() latency are not measured.
Behaviour with MonotonicLogStore implementations, which take the removeOldLogs branch instead of compactLogs.

result.summary:
Turn spent on the one open lead: whether an InstallSnapshot that is current in term but older in index can rewind a receiver's applied state. Instead of more reading I built the probe its discriminator called for and requested the fixed execution (valid:true).

Probe (draft/assurance_install_rewind.go): three rounds of 25 warm commands, isolate one follower, 60 further commands through the remaining quorum so the leader compacts past that follower's next index, reconnect, then 1.2s of polling every 2ms across all three nodes. It records each node's applied index, snapshot index and log store last index, tracks the maximum applied index seen, any applied-index decrease with the snapshot index and log store last index at that moment, snapshot-index changes, and how many poll ticks showed the snapshot index above the log store last index (the install signature). Per node it emits recovered_node_probe_end when that signature was seen and steady_node_probe_end otherwise, with all operands (prior/new applied index, decrease_count, indices at the decrease) so a negative or positive result is inspectable.

Experiment request: requirement stated as a protection (no delivered InstallSnapshot in this scenario moves a receiver's applied index backwards; a request whose snapshot index is below the receiver's applied state would appear as an applied-index decrease), responsibility at receiver-side admission and applied-state bookkeeping, anchors at Raft.installSnapshot (raft.go:1814-1950), Raft.processLogs (raft.go:1292-1358) and raftState.getLastIndex (state.go:159-163). Two comparisons, role-specific event names to avoid the correlation defect from the earlier successor: the recovered node (applicability install_signature_seen true) and the steady nodes in the same execution (install_signature_seen false), both asserting observed_applied_decrease false.

Native local feedback, flagged in the investigation limitations as not retained evidence: the probe reached the install state (recovered node snapshot index 257 above log store last index 197 for 1234 poll ticks) with applied state monotone (max 257, decrease_count 0) while the other two nodes reported no install signature — so locally the concern was not reproduced in this scenario. The investigation stays paused: the probe can refute the concern only for the scenarios it drives, and it does not construct the configuration where the leader's latest snapshot index is below a follower's applied index, so no defect claim is made either way.

investigations.question: In the captured snapshot, is a leadership-transfer order (TimeoutNow) bound at the receiver to the current leader's authority, or can a delivered order that carries no term and whose claimed sender is not the current leader (and not a configuration member) drive a stable follower out of Follower and depose the serving leader?
investigations.hypothesis: Raft.timeoutNow is the only RPC handler that changes authority without consulting any term: it does setLeader("",""), setState(Candidate) and candidateFromLeadershipTransfer.Store(true) and responds, ignoring RPCHeader.ID/Addr and the configuration. TimeoutNowRequest embeds only RPCHeader, so no term/freshness value exists to check, while the producer only sends it after it has caught the target up (nextIndex beyond the leader's last index) - a precondition the receiver cannot verify. The Candidate run skips pre-vote (raft.go:294-298) and voters skip the known-leader rejection for LeadershipTransfer candidates (raft.go:1645-1656), so the order withdraws both disruption guards at once.
investigations.discriminator: In one fault-free, normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with a stable leader at a known term, deliver a single TimeoutNow to a follower using a transport RPC header whose ID is not a configuration member (and which necessarily carries no term), then observe the target's state/term and the previous leader's state/term for a bounded interval. Control: the same non-member sender with a RequestVoteRequest that does carry a term, but an older one, must leave the target unchanged. If the TimeoutNow leaves the target in Follower at the same term and the leader in place, the hypothesis is refuted; if the target leaves Follower at a higher term while the leader steps down, the receiver-side authority gap is observed.
limitations: The witness is one execution of one fault-free in-process cluster; it establishes the receiver-side transition, not how long clients stayed without a leader afterwards.

Safety was not violated in this execution and is not claimed to be: term/vote rules still select the leader. The defect is the acceptance of a leadership-transfer order that is bound neither to the sender's identity/term nor to its configuration membership.

Because the order carries no term, a replayed or delayed order from a legitimate former leader is indistinguishable from the witness message at the receiver; the witness does not separate those two producers.

investigations.hypothesis: The branch is asymmetric with AddVoter: when the target server currently has Suffrage != Nonvoter (a voter or staging server) it writes only the address and keeps the existing suffrage, whereas AddVoter replaces the entry when the server is not already a voter. investigations.question: Can shouldSnapshot's unsigned delta between the log store's last index and the last snapshot index underflow, so that the automatic snapshot condition is permanently true on a node whose log store sits below its snapshot index, and what does such a node then do every SnapshotInterval?
investigations.hypothesis: shouldSnapshot computes delta := lastIdx - lastSnap with unsigned integers and no ordering check, where lastIdx is the log store's LastIndex and lastSnap is the snapshot index kept separately. A node that recovered through InstallSnapshot sets its last snapshot index to the snapshot's index, while its log store may keep a lower index: installSnapshot compacts with min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailingLogs), so a node whose log store is below the snapshot index keeps that lower index, and the node's snapshot-aware log index (getLastIndex = max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex)) does not feed shouldSnapshot. If a run reaches that state, delta underflows and the node takes a fresh full-state snapshot every SnapshotInterval until its log store grows past the snapshot index.
investigations.discriminator: Build a cluster whose leader has compacted most of its log, let a fresh or lagging follower recover by InstallSnapshot, and then record, per SnapshotInterval: the follower's log store FirstIndex/LastIndex, its last snapshot index, whether shouldSnapshot returned true, whether takeSnapshot created a new snapshot at the same index and whether a repeat install happened. A confirmed defect needs the log store index below the snapshot index together with repeated snapshot creation on an otherwise idle node; if the log store index is always at or above the snapshot index after install, or if some other producer raises it, the hypothesis is refuted.

investigations.question: When leadership is lost while a VerifyLeader request is outstanding, can the resulting future be completed twice or left permanently unanswered, given that replication goroutines still hold it and notify it onto the shared verify channel after the leader loop has already responded to the pending set?
investigations.hypothesis: A pending verify future lives in two owners at once: the leader loop's notify set (responded with ErrLeadershipLost by the step-down cleanup) and each replication goroutine's notify map (a separate map, cleared by notifyAll at the end of an RPC). A goroutine that notifies after the cleanup therefore pushes the same future back onto the shared verifyCh, where the follower or candidate loop will respond to it a second time.
investigations.discriminator: Trace who may call respond on a verifyFuture and with what synchronisation, and what happens to a future that a replication goroutine re-notifies after the step-down cleanup: a defect requires two concurrent responders (a data race on the responded flag or a double send on the error channel) or a future that is never completed. If respond is reachable only from the main goroutine holding the run loop, and the second arrival is answered under the same stateless reject rule, the sequence is ordered and idempotent, and the apparent double completion is refuted.
limitations: Source-only: no execution and no race-detector run was requested, so this explains the ownership and ordering rather than observing a concurrent step-down.
The analysis covers verifyFuture completion paths in the captured revision; it says nothing about other future types or about respond callers added later.
The timing window in which a replication goroutine notifies after the cleanup was reasoned from the code, not measured.

investigations.question: Can an InstallSnapshot whose term is current but whose snapshot index is older than the receiving node's applied state rewind that node's applied state, and is the rewind always covered by re-application from the surviving log so that no acknowledged applied entry is lost?
investigations.hypothesis: installSnapshot performs no comparison between the request's LastLogIndex and the receiving node's own lastApplied, last snapshot index or log store range: it rejects only an older term, restores the FSM from the requested snapshot, sets lastApplied and the last snapshot index to the request's values (a decrease when the request is older by index), replaces both configurations from the request, and then compacts or removes old logs according to that index. Recovering from such a rewind therefore depends on processLogs replaying entries from lastApplied+1 out of the surviving log; if the node's log no longer covers (request index, previously applied index] - for example because it had already compacted past the older snapshot index - those already-applied entries cannot be re-applied and the rewound state persists.
investigations.discriminator: Two-sided. Sender side: determine whether a leader can be induced to send a snapshot whose index is below the follower's applied index, given that a snapshot is only opened when the leader cannot produce entries from its nextIndex (below its compacted first index) and that nextIndex only moves on follower responses. Receiver side: instrument a node whose log store first index is above the index of a delivered snapshot and record lastApplied, the FSM-visible applied index and the log first index immediately before and after the install, then whether a later commit advance re-applies the gap. A defect needs a delivered request with snapshot index below the receiver's applied index together with a log that does not cover the gap, so that the applied index is not re-reached; if every delivered request has an index at or above the receiver's applied index, or the surviving log always covers the gap, the concern is refuted.
limitations: Source-only so far, plus one native local run of the probe (not retained evidence) in which the recovered node reached the install signature (snapshot index 257 above log store last index 197 over 1234 poll ticks) while no node showed an applied-index decrease.
The probe can only refute the concern for the scenarios it drives; it cannot prove unreachability across configurations where the leader's latest snapshot index is below a follower's applied index.
No defect is claimed while the question is open.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster; one control RPC (stale-term RequestVote from a non-member claimed sender) followed by one TimeoutNow from the same claimed sender to a follower, with bounded observation of target and leader state/term.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) performs real bootstrap: initial configuration entry, leader election and log replication through the in-memory transport.
Both RPCs are delivered over the in-memory transport with no packet loss, reordering or delay, so any observed transition is caused by the delivered request itself.
The sender identity in the RPC header ('ghost-not-in-config') is deliberately not a configuration member; the probe does not rely on the sender being reachable or registered.
The cluster is healthy before the probe: a leader is serving at a known term, which the harness records as steady_state.
excluded: Network-transport authentication, TLS and peer-identity properties outside the Raft layer.
State-machine safety (log matching, single vote per term) and any claim that the newly elected leader violates it.
Behaviour after the observation interval, further elections, and client-visible unavailability.

parameters.control_request_term: target term at steady state minus 1

basis.prefix: The harness builds the prefix itself with the captured test facilities: MakeCluster(3, t, nil) bootstraps a three-voter configuration through the in-memory transport, waits for a stable leader (c.Leader()), and records the leader id/address/term and the chosen follower's state/term as CA_EVENT steady_state. It then selects the follower's transport peer as sender and emits CA_EVENT control_stale_request_vote after delivering a RequestVoteRequest with Term = targetTerm-1 and RPCHeader.ID = 'ghost-not-in-config'. Only then does it deliver the single TimeoutNowRequest with the same RPC header (no term field exists) and emit CA_EVENT after_timeout_now after a bounded 2s observation of the target and the previous leader. No state is injected and no storage is pre-filled.

basis.responsibility: Receiver-side admission of a leadership-transfer order in Raft.timeoutNow, and the two guards that the order disables: the candidate pre-vote gate and the known-leader vote rejection.

comparisons.description: Control: a request that carries a stale term from the same non-member claimed sender is refused and leaves the target in Follower at its original term.
Probe: the delivered order moves the follower out of Follower and raises its term, although the order carries no term and its claimed sender is not the leader or a member.
Probe consequence: the previously serving leader is no longer Leader and reports a higher term within the bounded observation interval.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with a small SnapshotInterval/SnapshotThreshold/TrailingLogs: warm traffic, isolation of one follower, further traffic so the leader compacts, reconnection so the follower recovers by InstallSnapshot, then a bounded idle window on the recovered node (isolated again so no further InstallSnapshot can occur) with the leader observed over the same window as control.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) with SnapshotInterval=40ms, SnapshotThreshold=20, TrailingLogs=5 performs real bootstrap, replication, snapshots and log compaction through the in-memory transport.

Disconnecting only the chosen follower leaves the leader with a quorum (itself plus the other follower), so the cluster keeps committing and the leader's log compacts past the isolated follower's next index.
The isolated follower does not raise its term while isolated because pre-vote is active by default, so reconnecting lets the leader complete the recovery without a spurious election.
Isolating the recovered node again before the window removes the leader as a source of further snapshots, so any new snapshot in that node's store must be produced by its own snapshot goroutine.
Both observed nodes run the same configuration; the leader is idle in the window except for heartbeats.
excluded: Safety claims: no state-machine divergence, lost entry or double application is asserted.
Cost measurement: bytes written, disk wear and FSM Snapshot() latency are not measured.
Behaviour with MonotonicLogStore implementations, which take the removeOldLogs branch instead of compactLogs.
Duration of the condition under production SnapshotInterval values.

basis.prefix: The harness builds everything with captured test facilities and real producers: MakeCluster(3, conf) with SnapshotInterval=30ms, SnapshotThreshold=10, TrailingLogs=5 bootstraps the cluster and Elects a leader; each round applies 25 commands through leader.Apply, chooses the lexicographically first follower, records its applied index, snapshot index and log store last index, cuts it off with c.Disconnect, commits 60 further commands through the remaining quorum, reconnects with c.FullyConnect, and then polls all three nodes every 2ms for 1.2s. During polling the harness tracks each node's maximum applied index, any applied-index decrease with the snapshot index and log store last index at that moment, the number of snapshot-index changes, and how many poll ticks showed the snapshot index above the log store last index (the install signature). probe_start and one round_start per round record the scenario operands; per node the harness emits recovered_node_probe_end when the install signature was seen and steady_node_probe_end otherwise, carrying max_applied_seen, applied_at_end, observed_applied_decrease, decrease_count, the prior and new applied index and the snapshot/log index at the decrease, snapshot_index_changes, install_signature_ticks and the end state. No storage is pre-filled and no production code is modified.
basis.requirement: No InstallSnapshot delivered in this scenario moves a receiver's applied index backwards: a request whose snapshot index is below the receiver's applied state would show up as an applied-index decrease with the snapshot index below the previously observed applied index, and the receiver's applied index must stay monotone across the isolation, compaction and recovery rounds.
basis.responsibility: Receiver-side admission and applied-state bookkeeping of InstallSnapshot (lastApplied set from the request, snapshot index, log store range) observed through the values the node reports while the leader drives real installs.

comparisons.description: Recovered node: having been through the install path during the rounds, its applied index never moved backwards, so no delivered snapshot was older than its applied state in this execution.

Same-execution comparison: nodes that never showed the install signature kept applied state monotone as well, so a decrease would have to be attributed to the install path rather than to polling or snapshotting in general.
